questions.stem: A 49 year old man has a 6 hour history of severe abdominal pain that started suddenly in the upper abdomen. He takes naproxen for back pain. He is lying very still on the trolley and says that the ambulance journey over speed bumps was agony. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 116 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on abdominal examination?
o: Pain out of proportion with a soft, non-tender abdomen
Shifting dullness with a non-tender abdomen
Soft abdomen with a palpable mass in the right iliac fossa
Visible peristalsis with tinkling bowel sounds
questions.e: NSAID use, sudden upper abdominal pain and lying still because movement hurts point to a perforated peptic ulcer with generalised peritonitis, which gives a rigid, board-like abdomen.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely finding on abdominal examination?
NSAID plus sudden pain suggests perforation. Lying still and pain on movement are the behaviour of peritonitis.

elim: Classic of early acute mesenteric ischaemia, not a patient who lies still from peritoneal irritation.
Suggests uncomplicated ascites; there is no peritoneal irritation.
Suggests an appendix mass or caecal tumour, not a perforation.
Suggests mechanical obstruction; peritonitis gives a silent, rigid abdomen.

steps.x: Peritonitis = lies still, pain on movement, guarding, rebound and a board-like rigid abdomen.

questions.stem: A 77 year old man on the intensive care unit has had increasing abdominal distension and pain for 12 hours. He has a history of peptic ulcer disease and is too unwell to sit upright. A supine abdominal X-ray shows that both the inner and outer walls of several loops of bowel are clearly outlined by gas.
questions.q: Which is the most likely radiological sign shown?
questions.e: Gas outlining both the luminal and peritoneal sides of the bowel wall is Rigler's sign, which means free intraperitoneal gas from a perforated viscus.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely radiological sign shown?

clues: both the inner and outer walls
steps.x: Gas on both sides of the bowel wall on a supine film means air is inside and outside the bowel: free gas.

elim: A dilated twisted sigmoid loop in sigmoid volvulus, not gas on both sides of the bowel wall.
A comma-shaped dilated caecum in caecal volvulus.
Loss of haustra in chronic ulcerative colitis.
Thickened oedematous bowel wall in ischaemic or infective colitis.

steps.x: Rigler's sign = gas on both luminal and peritoneal sides of the bowel wall on AXR = perforation.

questions.stem: An 84 year old woman in a nursing home has a 1 day history of abdominal pain after several weeks of indigestion treated with ibuprofen. She is unable to stand for an erect film. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg. Her abdomen is tender with guarding. A supine abdominal X-ray shows Rigler's sign.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Rigler's sign shows free intraperitoneal gas; with NSAID use and dyspepsia the most likely source is a perforated peptic ulcer.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?
NSAID dyspepsia then pain and guarding; Rigler's sign confirms free gas, so a viscus has perforated.

elim: Gives small bowel obstruction with gas in the biliary tree, not gas on both sides of the bowel wall.
Gives dilated gas-filled loops but no free intraperitoneal gas.
Gives a coffee bean sign, not Rigler's sign.
Gives central dilated loops with air-fluid levels; no free gas unless it perforates.

steps.x: Rigler's sign = perforation; NSAIDs + dyspepsia = perforated peptic ulcer, the commonest cause of peritonitis.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis and ascites is admitted with increasing drowsiness. He has no fever. His abdomen is distended and mildly tender, with no guarding. His creatinine has risen from 88 to 162 µmol/L. A diagnostic ascitic tap is performed. Ascitic neutrophil count is shown below.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: An ascitic neutrophil count above 250 cells/µl in a patient with cirrhotic ascites confirms SBP, which often presents only with encephalopathy or kidney injury.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?
Cirrhosis with ascites plus new confusion or AKI: always tap the ascites. Neutrophils of 420 is above 250.

elim: Hepatic vein obstruction gives sudden ascites and hepatomegaly, not raised ascitic neutrophils.
Can follow SBP and explains the creatinine, but does not raise ascitic neutrophils.
Secondary peritonitis gives guarding and rigidity, and usually a polymicrobial ascitic fluid.
Causes worsening ascites and pain but not a raised ascitic neutrophil count.

steps.x: SBP = ascitic neutrophils >250 cells/µl. Fever and pain may be absent; confusion or AKI can be the only clue.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man has a 3 day history of abdominal pain. It began in his right iliac fossa but over the last 6 hours has spread across his whole abdomen. He has vomited twice. His temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 124 bpm and BP 108/64 mmHg. His abdomen is rigid with generalised guarding and rebound tenderness.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Generalised peritonitis from a perforated appendix
questions.e: Localised RIF pain that spreads to the whole abdomen with rigidity, fever and tachycardia means appendicitis has perforated and localised peritonitis has become generalised.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: began in his right iliac fossa
steps.x: Pain moving from local to generalised means containment has failed; rigidity means generalised peritonitis.

elim: A contained, localised process; it gives a tender RIF mass, not generalised rigidity.
Gives subacute RIF pain, diarrhoea and weight loss, not generalised peritonism over hours.
Follows a viral illness with mild RIF tenderness and no rigidity.
Loin to groin colic in a restless patient with a soft abdomen.

steps.x: Localised peritonitis (e.g. appendicitis) can become generalised if not contained.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man with known diverticulosis has had left iliac fossa pain for 2 days. This morning the pain suddenly became severe and generalised. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 100/60 mmHg. His abdomen is distended and rigid with rebound tenderness throughout. An erect chest X-ray shows free gas under the diaphragm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Diverticulitis that suddenly becomes generalised with rigidity and free gas has perforated, causing generalised peritonitis.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?
Diverticular disease plus a sudden change to generalised pain and free gas means perforation.

elim: Causes change in bowel habit and obstruction over weeks; sudden free gas is a later event.
A contained collection gives localised LIF tenderness and a mass, not free gas and generalised rigidity.
Gives left-sided pain and bloody diarrhoea, usually without free gas.
Gives massive distension and absolute constipation with a coffee bean sign.

steps.x: Perforated diverticulitis is a common cause of generalised peritonitis: free gas + rigidity.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman with atrial fibrillation, who stopped her apixaban a week ago, had sudden severe central abdominal pain 14 hours ago. Initially her abdomen was soft. It is now rigid with rebound tenderness. Her temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 130 bpm irregular and BP 92/58 mmHg. Investigations are shown below.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her peritonitis?
o: Acute mesenteric ischaemia with bowel infarction
questions.e: AF off anticoagulation with pain out of proportion to a soft abdomen, progressing to peritonitis and a high lactate, is mesenteric ischaemia that has infarcted.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely cause of her peritonitis?
An embolic source and soft-then-rigid abdomen means the bowel has died and peritonitis followed.

elim: Epigastric pain radiating to the back with a raised amylase; no embolic source story.
Rigid from the start, with NSAID or ulcer history; not soft early on.
Back pain, shock and a pulsatile mass, not peritonitis developing over hours.
Distension and constipation in a constipated patient, with a coffee bean sign.

steps.x: Bowel ischaemia is a cause of peritonitis: once the bowel infarcts, the abdomen becomes rigid.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man has a 4 day history of colicky abdominal pain, distension and absolute constipation from a known obstructing sigmoid tumour awaiting surgery. Over the last 2 hours his pain has become constant and severe. His temperature is 38.5°C and pulse rate 122 bpm. His abdomen is now rigid and silent on auscultation.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of the change in his condition?
o: Worsening of the closed obstruction without perforation
questions.e: A change from colicky to constant severe pain with rigidity, fever and a silent abdomen in obstruction means the bowel has perforated, causing peritonitis.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely cause of the change in his condition?
Colic means obstruction; constant pain plus rigidity means peritoneal irritation from perforation.

elim: Gives a tender suprapubic mass, not a rigid silent abdomen with fever.
Massive distension without a mechanical cause and without peritonism.
Painless distension and a quiet abdomen, without rigidity or fever.
Gives worsening colic and distension, not sudden constant pain with rigidity.

steps.x: Perforated bowel obstruction is a cause of peritonitis: colic turns constant, abdomen turns rigid.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man has generalised peritonitis from a perforated sigmoid diverticulum. He has guarding, rebound tenderness and a rigid abdomen. He was admitted 4 hours ago and has received IV fluids and IV antibiotics. He is being prepared for theatre and his observations are repeated.
questions.q: Which new finding would most indicate that his disease has become severe?
o: Rebound tenderness in the right iliac fossa
questions.e: Hypotension is a late and severe sign in peritonitis and suggests septic shock, which needs urgent resuscitation.

steps.x: The question asks: which new finding would most indicate that his disease has become severe?
He already has peritonitis; the question is which sign marks progression to shock.

elim: Tachycardia is an early, common sign of peritonitis rather than a marker of severe late disease.
An expected sign of parietal peritoneal irritation, not of severity.
Fever is common in peritonitis and does not on its own mark shock.
Vomiting is a usual feature of peritonitis.

steps.x: In peritonitis, hypotension is a late/severe sign: think septic shock and resuscitate now.

questions.stem: An 82 year old woman with dementia is brought from her care home with 2 days of vomiting and fever. Her abdomen is distended and she grimaces and guards when any part of it is pressed. Pressing and releasing quickly makes her cry out. Her temperature is 38.7°C and pulse rate 114 bpm. Investigations are shown below.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Generalised guarding and rebound tenderness with fever, vomiting, distension and high inflammatory markers mean generalised peritonitis, even when the history is limited by dementia.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: guards when any part of it is pressed
releasing quickly makes her cry out
steps.x: Guarding everywhere plus rebound plus fever and raised markers = generalised peritoneal inflammation.

elim: Gives right upper quadrant pain and Murphy's sign, not generalised guarding and rebound.
Gives a distended but soft abdomen without fever, guarding or rebound.
Vomiting and fever but a soft abdomen without guarding or rebound.
Suprapubic discomfort and confusion, not generalised guarding and rebound.

steps.x: Peritonitis: severe pain, guarding, rebound, rigidity, fever, vomiting, distension, raised inflammatory markers.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman has an 8 hour history of severe abdominal pain after an upper GI endoscopy with oesophageal dilatation earlier today. She has also had biliary colic in the past. Her temperature is 38.0°C and pulse rate 108 bpm. Her abdomen is tender with guarding.
questions.q: Which feature of the history would most support peritonitis?
o: Colicky pain that makes her roll around
Pain that came on after a fatty meal
Pain worse on coughing and moving
questions.e: Peritoneal inflammation makes any movement of the peritoneum painful, so patients lie still and pain is worse on coughing and movement.

steps.x: The question asks: which feature of the history would most support peritonitis?

clues: Her abdomen is tender with guarding
steps.x: Instrumentation can perforate a viscus. The history feature of peritonitis is pain on any movement.

elim: Restless writhing is typical of colic (biliary or renal), not peritonitis.
Typical of pancreatitis or pericarditis.
Classic of duodenal ulcer pain, not a perforation.
Suggests biliary colic or cholecystitis.

steps.x: Peritonitis: pain worse on movement and coughing; patients lie still. Colic: patients writhe.

questions.stem: A 54 year old man with COPD on long-term prednisolone has a 5 hour history of sudden severe epigastric pain. He drinks heavily. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 110 bpm, BP 124/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. His abdomen is rigid with guarding. Serum amylase is 140 U/L (25–125).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial imaging investigation?
questions.e: Suspected perforation (steroids, sudden pain, rigidity; amylase only mildly raised) needs an erect chest X-ray first to look for free air under the diaphragm.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate initial imaging investigation?
Steroids raise ulcer risk. A mildly raised amylase occurs in perforation and does not mean pancreatitis (that needs over 3 times normal).

elim: Useful for gallstones, but poor at showing free intraperitoneal gas.
Invasive and has no role in suspected perforation.
Slow and not used in the acute abdomen with suspected perforation.
Insufflating air into a perforated viscus is dangerous; not a first test.

steps.x: Suspected perforation: first imaging is an erect CXR for free air under the diaphragm.

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman has generalised abdominal pain, guarding and a temperature of 38.3°C. Her pulse rate is 102 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. An erect chest X-ray shows free air under the right hemidiaphragm. She has no ulcer symptoms and no NSAID use, and the site of the perforation is unclear.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to identify the underlying cause?
questions.e: Diagnosis of peritonitis is clinical, and CT abdomen and pelvis is the gold standard to find the underlying cause and plan surgery.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate investigation to identify the underlying cause?

clues: free air under the right hemidiaphragm
the site of the perforation is unclear
steps.x: Perforation is confirmed and she is stable; the question is the source, which CT shows.

elim: Operator-dependent and limited by gas; does not reliably show the source.
Barium leaking into the peritoneum causes severe peritonitis; contraindicated.
Insufflation could enlarge a perforation; not used acutely.
Already shows free air; repeating it adds nothing about the source.

steps.x: Peritonitis: clinical diagnosis + CT to identify the cause. Barium and endoscopy are dangerous in perforation.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has a 10 hour history of severe epigastric pain that is now spreading to his right iliac fossa. He takes aspirin and ibuprofen. His pulse rate is 106 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg. His upper abdomen is rigid. An erect chest X-ray shows no free air under the diaphragm.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate investigation?
o: Repeat erect chest X-ray in 24 hours
questions.e: A normal erect chest X-ray does not exclude perforation; with a rigid abdomen and NSAID use, CT abdomen and pelvis is next.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the next most appropriate investigation?

clues: no free air under the diaphragm
steps.x: High clinical suspicion with a negative CXR still needs CT; small perforations or sealed leaks can be missed.

elim: Less sensitive than CT for small amounts of free gas and does not show the source.
Unsafe; a rigid abdomen needs inpatient imaging.
Delays diagnosis while a perforation leaks.
Tests for H. pylori, not for perforation.

steps.x: Erect CXR first; if normal but suspicion high, go to CT abdomen/pelvis.

questions.stem: A 56 year old woman with cirrhosis and tense ascites has abdominal discomfort and a temperature of 37.9°C. Her abdomen is distended with mild generalised tenderness and no guarding. A diagnostic paracentesis is performed and the fluid is sent for analysis.
questions.q: Which ascitic fluid result would confirm the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is diagnosed by paracentesis and confirmed by an ascitic neutrophil count above 250 cells/µl.

steps.x: The question asks: which ascitic fluid result would confirm the most likely diagnosis?
Cirrhosis plus ascites plus mild fever and tenderness without guarding is SBP until proven otherwise.

elim: A high protein suggests a cardiac or malignant cause of ascites, not infection.
Suggests bloody tap, trauma or malignancy.
Indicates portal hypertension as the cause of ascites, not infection.
Indicates chylous ascites.

steps.x: SBP threshold: ascitic neutrophils >250 cells/µl.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis and ascites is admitted after a fall. Over 48 hours he becomes more confused and his creatinine rises from 92 to 170 µmol/L. He has no fever and his abdomen is distended but only mildly tender. Urine dipstick is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: Diagnostic ascitic tap for neutrophil count and culture
questions.e: In cirrhosis with ascites, new confusion or AKI may be the only sign of SBP, so a diagnostic paracentesis for neutrophil count and culture is needed.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
Any deterioration in a cirrhotic with ascites needs an ascitic tap, even without fever or pain.

elim: Confirms ascites but cannot show that it is infected.
Worth considering after a fall, but does not explain the AKI or test the ascites.
Excludes obstruction but misses the treatable cause here.
Does not change management and does not identify the precipitant.

steps.x: SBP is diagnosed by paracentesis: neutrophils >250 cells/µl, send culture.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man has a perforated duodenal ulcer on erect chest X-ray. He has generalised guarding. His temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 116/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. The surgical registrar has been called.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Nil by mouth, oxygen, IV fluids and IV broad-spectrum antibiotics
Oral fluids and analgesia then review in the morning
Triple therapy for H. pylori eradication
questions.e: Immediate management of peritonitis is NBM, IV fluids, oxygen and broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, with urgent surgical review for source control.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate initial management?
ABCDE: hypoxic and tachycardic with peritonitis. Resuscitate and start IV antibiotics while surgery is arranged.

elim: Peritonitis needs immediate resuscitation, not delay.
Oral drugs are inappropriate: he must be nil by mouth and needs IV treatment.
Part of later ulcer care, not emergency treatment of peritonitis.
Air insufflation can worsen a perforation; not the immediate step.

steps.x: Peritonitis first steps: NBM, IV fluids, O2, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, urgent surgical review.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman has peritonitis from a perforated appendix and is waiting 2 hours for theatre. She has received IV fluids, oxygen and IV antibiotics. She has vomited four times in the last hour and her abdomen is increasingly distended. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 120/70 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Supportive care in peritonitis includes analgesia and a nasogastric tube when there is vomiting and distension, to decompress the stomach and reduce aspiration risk.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the next most appropriate step in management?

clues: received IV fluids, oxygen and IV antibiotics
steps.x: Resuscitation is done. Ongoing vomiting and distension needs gastric decompression.

elim: Not used in peritonitis and may worsen a perforation.
Laxatives have no role and she is nil by mouth.
She is nil by mouth and needs decompression, not an oral drug.
Used to decompress sigmoid volvulus, not peritonitis.

steps.x: Supportive care in peritonitis: analgesia, plus an NG tube if vomiting or distended.

questions.stem: A 38 year old man has suspected peritonitis with a rigid abdomen. He is in severe pain and is distressed. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg. The foundation doctor is told not to give anything for pain until the consultant has examined him in 3 hours.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management of his pain?
o: No analgesia until the consultant has examined him
questions.e: Analgesia is part of supportive care in peritonitis and does not mask the clinical signs; titrated IV opioid is appropriate for severe pain.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate management of his pain?

clues: not to give anything for pain
steps.x: Withholding analgesia is an old myth. He is NBM, so give IV.

elim: An NSAID may worsen a perforated ulcer and kidney injury in sepsis.
Analgesia does not mask the diagnosis and should not be withheld.
He should be nil by mouth and oral absorption is unreliable.
Inadequate for severe pain and he should be nil by mouth.

steps.x: Peritonitis supportive care includes analgesia: titrated IV opioid; never withhold it.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has a CT showing perforated sigmoid diverticulitis with free faecal fluid throughout the abdomen. He has generalised peritonitis. He has received IV fluids, oxygen and IV antibiotics. His pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 108/68 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: Emergency laparotomy with sigmoid resection and end colostomy
questions.e: Definitive management of peritonitis is source control; free faecal contamination needs laparotomy, resection and stoma (Hartmann's procedure).

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate definitive management?

clues: free faecal fluid throughout the abdomen
steps.x: Generalised faecal contamination cannot be drained by a needle; it needs an operation.

elim: Endoscopy risks enlarging the perforation and does not clean the abdomen.
Suits a contained diverticular abscess, not free faecal peritonitis.
Antibiotics without source control fail in faecal peritonitis.
Decompresses sigmoid volvulus; no role here.

steps.x: Definitive treatment of peritonitis = treat the cause: surgery, drainage or repair (source control).

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman is 5 days after an appendicectomy for a perforated appendix. She has a swinging fever and lower abdominal pain. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. She has tenderness and guarding in the suprapubic region only. CT shows a 6 cm rim-enhancing pelvic collection.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Image-guided drainage of the collection with IV antibiotics
questions.e: A localised post-operative pelvic abscess is source-controlled by radiological drainage with IV antibiotics; laparotomy is not needed while it is contained.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate management?
Localised peritonitis with a contained collection: drain it.

elim: A 6 cm abscess needs drainage; oral antibiotics alone will fail.
Delays source control while she is septic.
Used for sigmoid volvulus.
Far too radical for a localised collection.

steps.x: Source control includes drainage of a contained collection, not always laparotomy.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman with cirrhosis and ascites is ready for discharge after treatment for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Her ascitic culture grew E. coli, which responded to IV cefotaxime. Her ascites is controlled on spironolactone. She asks what will stop the infection coming back.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
questions.e: After an episode of SBP, long-term antibiotic prophylaxis with ciprofloxacin reduces recurrence.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate long-term management?

clues: what will stop the infection coming back
steps.x: This is secondary prevention of SBP, which means an oral antibiotic.

elim: Prevents hepatic encephalopathy, not recurrent SBP.
Primary prophylaxis of variceal bleeding.
Large-volume taps treat tense ascites but do not prevent infection.
Used to prevent hepatic encephalopathy recurrence.

steps.x: Post-SBP: antibiotic prophylaxis with ciprofloxacin.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man has generalised peritonitis from a perforated duodenal ulcer. One hour after admission his BP is 82/48 mmHg, pulse rate 128 bpm and urine output 10 mL in the last hour. He has not yet received any fluids or antibiotics. Venous lactate is 5.4 mmol/L (0.5–2.0).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
o: IV fluid bolus and IV broad-spectrum antibiotics
IV furosemide for the low urine output
Oral antibiotics and repeat lactate in 4 hours
Wait for blood culture results before antibiotics
questions.e: Hypotension, oliguria and rising lactate mean septic shock secondary to peritonitis, which needs urgent resuscitation with IV fluids and IV broad-spectrum antibiotics before source control.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate immediate management?

clues: not yet received any fluids or antibiotics
steps.x: Shock, oliguria and high lactate: septic shock. Resuscitate first, then source control.

elim: Imaging must not delay resuscitation of septic shock.
Oliguria here is from shock; a diuretic would worsen hypoperfusion.
Too slow and he is nil by mouth.
Antibiotics should be given within the hour; take cultures but do not wait.

steps.x: Peritonitis + hypotension, oliguria, rising lactate = septic shock: urgent fluids and IV antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman has generalised peritonitis from perforated diverticulitis. Despite 2 litres of IV fluid her BP is 78/44 mmHg and pulse rate 132 bpm. She is warm peripherally with a temperature of 38.9°C. Her urine output is 5 mL per hour and lactate 6.2 mmol/L (0.5–2.0). Her haemoglobin is 128 g/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her hypotension?
questions.e: Fever, warm peripheries, hypotension despite fluids, oliguria and high lactate in peritonitis are septic shock, from the systemic inflammatory response to peritoneal contamination.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely cause of her hypotension?
Warm, febrile, fluid-resistant hypotension with a source in the abdomen is distributive shock from sepsis.

elim: No allergen, rash, wheeze or angioedema.
Gives cold peripheries and pulmonary oedema, not warm, febrile shock.
Her haemoglobin is normal and there is no bleeding source.
Follows spinal cord injury and gives bradycardia, not tachycardia.

steps.x: Peritonitis can cause septic shock: hypotension, oliguria, rising lactate. Resuscitate urgently.

questions.stem: A 41 year old man has had sudden severe epigastric pain for 2 hours. He takes ibuprofen daily. His abdomen is rigid and an erect chest X-ray shows free air under the diaphragm. At laparoscopy there is bile-stained fluid but no pus. The surgeon explains how the peritonitis developed so quickly.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his peritonitis at this early stage?
o: Bacterial translocation across an intact bowel wall
Chemical irritation of the peritoneum by gastric and duodenal contents
Haematogenous spread of bacteria to the peritoneum
Ischaemic necrosis of the parietal peritoneum
questions.e: Hollow viscus perforation releases GI contents; in a perforated ulcer, acid and bile cause chemical peritonitis first, with bacterial contamination following later.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely mechanism of his peritonitis at this early stage?

clues: sudden severe epigastric pain for 2 hours
steps.x: Two hours after perforation with no pus: the inflammation is chemical, from leaked acid and bile.

elim: Serositis occurs in SLE and is not caused by perforation.
The mechanism of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, which has no perforation.
Proposed for SBP; not the cause after perforation.
The parietal peritoneum is not ischaemic in a perforated ulcer.

steps.x: Peritonitis = bacterial contamination or chemical irritation, most often after hollow viscus perforation.

questions.stem: A 65 year old man has had generalised peritonitis for 24 hours. He has received no fluids. His pulse rate is 124 bpm and BP 96/60 mmHg. His mucous membranes are dry and his urine is concentrated. He has not vomited much or had diarrhoea, yet his urea has risen to 14.8 mmol/L (2.5–7.8).
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his dehydration?
o: Third-space fluid loss from widespread peritoneal inflammation
questions.e: Generalised peritoneal inflammation causes fluid shifts into the peritoneal cavity and bowel (third-spacing), giving intravascular depletion without obvious external losses.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely mechanism of his dehydration?
He is dry without external losses, so fluid has moved into the inflamed peritoneum and bowel.

elim: Possible in long-term steroid users but not suggested here.
No haematemesis or melaena; urea would rise with a bleed but the story does not fit.
No diabetes or glycosuria described.
Causes euvolaemic hyponatraemia, not dehydration and hypotension.

steps.x: Generalised peritonitis causes widespread inflammation, third-spacing and a systemic inflammatory response.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman has a 2 day history of right iliac fossa pain. As the doctor palpates her right iliac fossa, the muscles of her abdominal wall tighten involuntarily beneath the hand, even when she is distracted. She is not anxious and says she is trying to relax. Her temperature is 38.1°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of this sign?
o: Distension of the bowel by gas
Referred visceral pain via T10 dermatome
Reflex contraction of the abdominal wall muscles over inflamed peritoneum
questions.e: Guarding is reflex contraction of abdominal wall muscles in response to an inflamed parietal peritoneum; rebound tenderness is irritation felt when pressure is released.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely mechanism of this sign?
Involuntary tightening on palpation, persisting despite distraction, is true guarding.

elim: Causes distension and tympany, not involuntary muscle tightening.
Causes loss of liver dullness, not muscle contraction.
Explains periumbilical early appendicitis pain, not a muscle reflex.
She is relaxed and distracted; the tightening is involuntary.

steps.x: Guarding = reflex abdominal wall muscle contraction. Rebound = parietal peritoneal irritation on release.

questions.stem: A 53 year old man with hepatitis C cirrhosis and ascites has a fever of 38.2°C and diffuse abdominal tenderness without guarding. Diagnostic paracentesis shows cloudy fluid with a neutrophil count of 610 cells/µl (<250). Gram stain shows Gram-negative rods. There is no free gas on imaging.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: E. coli is the most common organism cultured from ascitic fluid in spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely causative organism?
Neutrophils above 250 with no perforation is SBP; a single Gram-negative rod is gut-derived.

elim: An anaerobe found in polymicrobial secondary peritonitis after perforation, not SBP.
Fungal peritonitis is rare and would not appear as Gram-negative rods.
A gas-forming anaerobe of gas gangrene, not a cause of SBP.
A Gram-positive coccus; seen with dialysis catheters, not classic SBP.

questions.stem: A 60 year old woman with alcohol-related cirrhosis and ascites has spontaneous bacterial peritonitis confirmed on paracentesis. CT shows no perforation, abscess or bowel abnormality. Her daughter asks how bacteria could reach the abdominal fluid when the bowel has no hole in it.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Bacterial translocation from the gut lumen across the bowel wall
Leakage of bile through the liver capsule
Spread from an infected urinary tract
questions.e: In ascites from cirrhosis, SBP is thought to result from bacteria translocating across the gut wall (or haematogenous spread), without any perforation.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely mechanism?
No perforation and ascites in cirrhosis: the bacteria cross an intact but leaky gut wall.

elim: SBP is spontaneous and occurs without instrumentation.
Bile peritonitis follows biliary injury; it is not bacterial translocation.
CT shows no perforation and this would be secondary peritonitis.
The urinary tract is not the usual source of SBP.

steps.x: SBP = ascites (usually cirrhosis) + bacterial translocation or haematogenous spread; no perforation.
